 Lafayette vs. Lehigh football: Leopards still have a lot to play for in 162nd meeting

 Easton graduate and Lafayette senior Sean Wilson is likely playing his last game at Fisher Stadium on Saturday when the Leopards welcome Lehigh in the 162nd edition of college football’s most-played rivalry. (Keith Groller)
 By Keith Groller | kgroller@mcall.com | The Morning Call PUBLISHED: November 18, 2026 at 7:30 PM EST | UPDATED: November 19, 2026 at 4:34 AM EST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Last year, Lafayette battled Lehigh deep into the fourth quarter but couldn’t get enough stops in a 42-32 loss that allowed the Mountain Hawks to cap a 12-0 regular season and secure the Patriot League championship and automatic FCS playoff berth.
 Had Lafayette, which actually led 17-14 at halftime, been able to hold on, they would have been able to claim the league title and head to the FCS tournament.
 This year, the Leopards are long out of the championship race and at 4-6 overall, 3-4 league, they know they will be packing up the uniforms once Saturday’s 162nd edition of college football’s most-played rivalry is over at Fisher Stadium.
 But make no mistake, Lafayette wants to sour Lehigh’s championship celebration and send them into the postseason on a down note.
 The Leopards also would like to claim the Lehigh Valley version of the Patriot League championship. It has been said that this one special game is a season all unto itself and the Leopards would love to savor this second season.
 “We’re excited,” said Lafayette coach John Troxell. “This is the most exciting day of the season every year. It’s why a lot of kids choose to come to Lafayette or Lehigh. It’s a big day for our alums, for our fans, for our kids. It’s something they’re going to remember forever. I remember being a player here and now I look at the guys who are coming back and how they reach out and you realize how important it is for our entire community.”
 Kickoff is set for 12:30 p.m. Saturday and while the game isn’t a sellout this year, it will still be viewed by alums across the country.
 Troxell said the game has special meaning for so many, and the current players need to realize that they’re not just playing for themselves, but for so many others.
 “I’ve got a guy who I played with here named John Carter and John has MS and he’s in a wheelchair, but he’ll be coming in from Sweden,” Troxell said. “There’s another guy named Mike Grau, a Pittsburgh guy who has been battling cancer and it’s in all parts of his body and he’s battling, and where does he want to be on Saturday? Right here, watching our kids play Lehigh and being around his boys. He was a great teammate.”
 Troxell said there’s another Lafayette alum, Matt Sala, who has been battling stage 4 colon cancer and while he lives in Hawaii he wants to be at the game.
 “He wants to be here because this is home and he wants to be around his guys, and when you think about it, that’s what it’s all about,” Troxell said.
 The season didn’t get started the way Lafayette wanted. The opener at Georgetown got cancelled by lightning at halftime. That was followed by a 56-7 loss at UConn. After a win over Marist, the Leopards suffered through a three-game losing streak that featured winnable games decided by a total of 23 points.
 “You look at that three-game stretch and we had an overtime loss at Columbia and games against Holy Cross and Richmond where we lost by a score,” Troxell said. “Those are games that can change your season if you win them. We were 1-4 at one point and the kids could have folded the tent, but the kids kept fighting and got us back to 4-6. I am proud of what the kids did to get us back to this point because they kept fighting, fighting and fighting. They didn’t quit. A win in this game can erase a lot of the heartache we’ve had through the course of the year. You go 1-10 and you beat Lehigh, it’s a successful season.”
 Sean Wilson, a senior left tackle from Easton, has been on the local football stage for eight years. He knows Saturday — win or lose — will be emotional.
 Motivation is never a problem for this game, Wilson said, but Troxell gave the team some other things to think about.
 “He fired us up right away telling us about all the alumni who are coming in and four or five of them are battling cancer or battling paralysis, things like that,” Wilson said. “Despite what they’re going through, they’re coming in to support us. They want to see a good game. They want to see us produce. That definitely got us fired up.”
 Looking at film got Wilson and the players even more fired up.
 “We were in the film room and we saw how violent this needs to be,” Wilson said. “We know we have to play with composure and with a will to hunt. Each time we’re out there on the field for eight seconds each play, we have to be ready because we’re going to war on Saturday.”
 Wilson is the first to admit the team has gone through some ups and downs. It started when several players left in the transfer portal in the offseason and then injuries took a toll.
 “Ethan Weber, our senior running back who did a really good job for us, came back from his ACL and then got a concussion, and then he came back from that and got another concussion,” Wilson said. “So, we lost him and went through a switch at quarterback. So, it has been a battle, but we’re still making sure that each time we’re on the field that we’re battling. Each week we want to go 1-0 and we have one more chance to do that.”
 Wilson has been happy to stay in his hometown throughout his college career.
 “One of the main reasons I stayed out of the portal is to get my degree from here,” he said. “It means a lot to me. It’s a great institution.”
 And he put in a plug for his high school alma mater, which was in the news for not necessarily all the right reasons this year.
 “A lot of people have some things to say about Easton and how they are and how the school is run and so on,” Wilson said. “But I just want to prove them wrong. I had a lot of doubters going into my high school career and whether I would get into college or not. I wanted to prove everyone wrong who doubted me and my family. I wanted to show them that I can do it and will do it and now I am excited for my next steps. No matter what, I have had a great four years here.”
